lectures.title: What is Single Source Shortest Path Problem?

cues.en: All right.
In this lecture we are going to talk about single source shortest path problem.
Now what does it mean.
So by definition a single source shortest path problem is about finding a path between a given vertex,
which is called source vertex, to all other vertices in a graph such that the total distance between
them is minimum.
So this means that the distance from the source to the destination has to be minimum.
So let's say we have a graph like this.
So in this graph we can take any vertex as a source.
So let's say we are taking as a source vertex a.
So we need to find out the shortest path from A to B from A to C, from A to D and from A to E.
Now here the most important point is that we need to find out the shortest path.
For example, to be able to go to from A to E, we can go from A to B, then E, or we can go to A to
D or E, or we can go to A to C, then D, then E.
So which one is the shortest path.
So by solving single source shortest path problem we can find it.
So the question is how can we solve this.
So we can solve this by using the breadth first search algorithm, Dijkstra's algorithm, and Bellman-ford
algorithm.
Now we are going to talk about them separately.
Now, before continuing to solve this problem, let's make it more clear by giving the real life example.
So let's say in real life we have a head office in one city and we have different branches in different

lectures.title: Why BFS does not for Work Weighted Graph?

cues.en: So in this lecture we are going to look at why breadth first search algorithm does not work with weighted
graph.
So in the previous lecture I have shown you how it works for unweighted graph.
But if the graph has weights associated with its edge, in this case it's not possible to find the single
source shortest path problem using the BFS.
So the question is why it is not working for weighted graph.
So this is the graph that we used in the previous lecture to find out the shortest path.
So from a we can go to B from A we can go to C.
And to be able to go to E from A we need to go to B, then E.
Now this is the only way that BFS finds the path from A to any other vertices.
Now if we put the weights over here and rerun the BFS, it's going to give us the same result.
But if you look at these weights, for example from A to D, it takes five minutes to go.
But there is an alternative way which takes the four unit.
For example we can go to from A to C, then d.
This is going to take four units.
Now similarly we can go to from A to B then D and this is going to take four units.
So this is the shortest path from going to directly from A to D.
So BFS cannot sort this out because we have already visited D.
So we are not going to come to D from C because it's already visited, and if it is visited we are marking
it as visited and we are not coming back to that node from any other vertices.
That's why BFS fails to find the single source shortest path problem using weighted graph.
So for this we have other algorithms like Dijkstra's algorithm and Bellman-ford algorithms which find
single source shortest path problem for weighted graph.
